title: A deep learning framework for recognizing skin changes secondary to chronic venous insufficiency in clinical photographs: a multicentre validation study

sections.title: 研究问题
sections.text:
《A deep learning framework for recognizing skin changes secondary to chronic venous insufficiency in clinical photographs: a multicentre validation study》：研究问题的原文依据。

【Introduction · S0001-p2】CVD is assessed according to the clinical, etiological, anatomical and pathophysiological (CEAP) classification [8]. The CEAP classification provides a standardized framework for describing these diverse presentations, with clinical stages defined as follows: C0 (no visible or palpable signs of venous disease), C1 (telangiectasias or reticular veins), C2 (varicose veins), C3 (oedema), C4 (skin and subcutaneous changes including pigmentation, eczema, lipodermatosclerosis (LDS) or corona phlebectatica), C5 (healed venous ulcer) and C6 (active venous ulcer) (Table 1). The term chronic venous insufficiency (CVI) is generally reserved for advanced stages (C3–C6), which involve significant tissue damage and oedema [9]. Clinically, distinguishing CVI-related lesions from other dermatoses is crucial because it directly influences management pathways and referral decisions. For example, if a patient with suspected CVD presents with a skin ulcer, the primary diagnostic objective is to determine whether the ulcer is caused by venous insufficiency. If so, venous interventions or surgery should be considered in addition to conservative treatment [10]. Conversely, if the skin lesion is not due to venous insufficiency but rather to another dermatological condition, the patient should consult a dermatologist and pursue a different treatment plan.

【Introduction · S0001-p5】Using a comprehensive clinical photo dataset encompassing a wide range of lower-extremity dermatoses, this study aims to develop and validate a deep learning model for binary classification that distinguishes CVI-related cutaneous manifestations from non-CVI skin conditions. The proposed algorithm is intended to provide an objective, reproducible decision-support tool for clinicians across diverse clinical backgrounds, thereby enhancing diagnostic consistency, standardizing clinical phenotyping and facilitating timely referral in the real-world management of CVD.

sections.title: 研究方法
sections.text:
《A deep learning framework for recognizing skin changes secondary to chronic venous insufficiency in clinical photographs: a multicentre validation study》：方法与研究设计的原文依据。

【Experimental design and model selection · S0002-S2006-p1】To determine the optimal configuration for CVI classification, we systematically evaluated several technical components. First, we compared multiple representative deep learning models, including ResNet-34 [29], ResNet-101 [29], ConvNeXt [30], Vision Transformer (ViT-B/16) [31] and Swin Transformer (Swin-T) [32], all trained under identical conditions to ensure a fair comparison. The influence of image resolution was further investigated by resizing images to 256 × 256, 512 × 512 and 1024 × 1024 pixels using the selected ResNet-34 backbone.

【Experimental design and model selection · S0002-S2006-p2】Regarding preprocessing, performance was evaluated under three configurations: training on resized raw images, using full-frame images with skin segmentation masks, and employing a pose-guided skin segmentation pipeline that localizes the lower extremities before applying masks. Finally, to assess generalizability, we compared models trained on a single-centre dataset (KUGH) against those trained on a multicentre dataset (KUGH, CAUGH and HVC). Evaluations were conducted on an internal test set, an external clinical dataset (KUAH) and the publicly available Fitzpatrick17k dataset [33]. For the Fitzpatrick17k evaluation, 38 of 69 images labelled as stasis oedema were included, while images of non-lower-extremity sites or those with extensive ulceration were excluded to maintain consistency with our study criteria. Since the refined Fitzpatrick17k dataset consists exclusively of positive cases for stasis oedema, performance was evaluated solely based on sensitivity. We additionally compared four oversampling strategies for handling class imbalance – Unweighted, Dataset-balanced, Class-balanced and Internal-only – and selected Dataset-balanced, which achieved the best balance between AUROC and CVI sensitivity on the validation set (Supplementary Table 3). All reported metrics represent the average performance over five independent runs.

All reported metrics represent the average performance over five independent runs.

sections.title: 主要结果
sections.text:
《A deep learning framework for recognizing skin changes secondary to chronic venous insufficiency in clinical photographs: a multicentre validation study》：结果的原文依据；数值与适用人群以引文为准。

【Impact of multicentre training and external validation · S0003-S2005-p1】Multicentre training improved discriminative performance across evaluation settings (Table 7). Specifically, AUROC on the internal KUGH test set increased from 0.889 to 0.922 (Δ AUROC = 0.033), and external validation on the KUAH dataset improved from 0.860 to 0.877. On the KUAH dataset, the multicentre-trained model achieved a sensitivity of 0.764 and an accuracy of 0.817. The confusion matrices for both internal and external validation (Figure 6) demonstrate that overall class-wise performance was well-preserved across datasets, with the majority of non-CVI-related dermatoses being correctly separated from CVI-related categories

【Impact of multicentre training and external validation · S0003-S2005-p2】On the Fitzpatrick17k dataset, sensitivity increased from 0.474 to 0.918. Performance stratified by Fitzpatrick skin type is shown in Figure 7; sensitivity was high for skin types I–V. Type VI was not evaluated, as only a single image (n = 1) was available for this skin type, which is insufficient to provide a meaningful performance estimate.
